claims.text: Multi-element mixing in refractory high-entropy alloys introduces intrinsic lattice distortion.
Lattice distortion caused by multi-element mixing enhances short-range order.
Short-range order raises barriers to dislocation activity and increases strength.
Short-range order robustly pins edge dislocations in refractory high-entropy alloys at elevated temperatures.
Edge dislocations are responsible for the high strength and strength retention of NbTaTiV and related BCC refractory high-entropy alloys at high temperature.
Severe lattice distortion itself raises the energy barriers for dislocation motion.
The NbTaTiV example is a disordered, multicomponent BCC solid solution.
NbTaTiV has significant atomic-size differences among its constituents.
A single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy can remain phase-stable to approximately 900°C.
The proposed mechanism remains applicable above 900°C.
Refractory high-entropy alloys can exhibit high yield strength, plasticity, and resistance to elevated-temperature softening.
The refractory HEA will retain greater high-temperature yield strength than a lower-entropy conventional refractory alloy of similar average composition.
The refractory HEA will contain a higher density of immobile or slowly propagating dislocation segments than the baseline alloy.
BCC refractory high-entropy alloys exhibit distinctive lattice-strain and elastic-anisotropy evolution at elevated temperature, with less temperature dependence than conventional metallic materials.
The proposed conventional binary or ternary baseline lacks the extensive lattice distortion and short-range order attributed to the HEA.
A lack of statistically significant improvements in strength retention, dislocation pinning, and thermoelastic response relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.
Evidence that lattice distortion does not materially modify dislocation dynamics would falsify the proposed causal mechanism.
